source_title: India’s Business Activity Rises, But Hiring Stalls - LinkedIn
source_excerpt:
India’s business activity hit a 4-month high, but hiring almost stopped. 📈👨💼 India’s Flash Composite PMI rose from 55.9 in September to 56.7 in October, showing stronger private-sector expansion. Services led the growth, while manufacturing softened slightly. The surprising part? Services employment was unchanged, ending a 9-month hiring streak. Companies said existing staff were enough to handle higher workloads, meaning more orders were being managed with roughly the same workforce. So the key lesson is simple: Economic Growth ↑ does not always mean Job Growth ↑ at the same pace. One month of PMI data is not enough to declare “jobless growth,” but it does highlight the growing gap between strong macro indicators and what job seekers may actually feel. #IndianEconomy #PMI #Employment #JobGrowth #BusinessActivity #ServicesSector #Manufacturing #EconomicGrowth #Jobs #Economics #Ecoholics
Kratik Rana 1w Report this post India's businesses are growing faster. Hiring isn't keeping up. India's latest business numbers tell an interesting story. According to the HSBC Flash India PMI released on October 23, private-sector business activity reached a four-month high. The Composite PMI rose from 55.9 in September to 56.7 in October. More orders. Stronger demand. Faster business activity. Sounds like good news for the job market, right? Not necessarily. The same survey found that employment growth had slowed to its weakest pace this year. Services companies reported no change in staffing levels, ending nine consecutive months of job creation. Businesses were handling additional workloads largely with their existing teams. What caught my attention is the difference between business growth and employment growth. We often assume that when companies grow, hiring naturally follows. But growth can also come from better utilisation of existing capacity, improved processes or simply working through outstanding orders. That doesn't mean new jobs won't follow. These are preliminary survey findings, not a prediction of future employment. It's a reminder that one positive economic indicator doesn't automatically mean every part of the economy is improving at the same pace. #IndianEconomy #JobMarket #BusinessGrowth #EconomicTrends #MarketResearch #BusinessInsights View C2PA information 1 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Infonions 3 followers 1w Report this post India’s private sector is growing at its fastest pace in four months. But job creation is slowing. That contrast is the important takeaway from the latest HSBC Flash India Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI), released on October 23. Here’s what the survey found for October: - Composite PMI: 56.7, up from 55.9 in September. - Services PMI: 56.2, up from 55.2. - Manufacturing PMI: 54.9, down slightly from 55.1. - Hiring: Employment grew at its slowest pace of 2026 so far, with services-sector staffing unchanged. A PMI reading above 50 signals expansion. So this is not a picture of a contracting private sector. Businesses are receiving more orders, and export orders recorded their fastest growth in six months. Why isn’t hiring rising at the same pace? The survey suggests that many companies believe their existing teams can handle current workloads. Outstanding work also declined, indicating that businesses were working through backlogs rather than accumulating more unfinished work. That creates an important distinction: More business activity does not automatically mean more vacancies. Companies can increase output by winning new orders, using existing capacity more efficiently or improving processes. Hiring depends on whether they need additional people to meet demand. What should job seekers take from this? 1. Follow demand in your target industry. Services and manufacturing are expanding, but hiring conditions differ across sectors and employers. 2. Show how you can contribute. Demonstrate relevant skills, completed projects and measurable improvements rather than relying on a list of tools alone. 3. Don’t interpret one survey as a jobs forecast. PMI is an early business-activity indicator, not a count of vacancies or a guarantee of future employment. The positive signal is that business demand is improving. The caution is that companies are not translating that improvement into hiring at the same pace. For anyone looking for a job, the question is not just whether the economy is growing. It is where companies need additional people, and what those companies need them to do. #IndianEconomy #JobMarket #HiringTrends #BusinessNews #Infonions 1 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in

Aastha Patil 6d Edited Report this post Indian businesses are growing. So why aren't they hiring more people? This is a question I think deserves more attention. India's Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) rose from 55.9 in September to 56.7 in October 2026, marking its fastest expansion in four months. Yet, job creation slowed to its weakest pace of the year. Here's what caught my attention. 1. Growth doesn't automatically translate into jobs. Businesses are handling higher workloads without expanding their workforce at the same pace. This could reflect better capacity utilisation, improved processes, or a greater focus on productivity. 2. Efficiency is becoming a bigger priority. Unfinished work fell at its joint-fastest pace in nearly six and a half years. Companies reported that their existing teams could handle the workload. For businesses, this can mean better operational efficiency. But it also raises questions about when additional demand will actually translate into new hiring. 3. The bigger challenge is sustainable growth. Slower cost pressures and improving business confidence are encouraging signs. However, if businesses continue expanding without creating proportionate employment opportunities, the benefits of economic growth may not reach enough people. That doesn't necessarily mean companies are replacing workers or that jobs are disappearing. One month's data cannot establish that. But it does highlight an important distinction: A growing economy and a growing job market are not always the same thing. The real question isn't just how fast Indian businesses are growing. It's whether that growth will generate enough new opportunities for India's workforce. Because ultimately, economic progress should be measured not only by business activity, but also by the opportunities it creates. Source: Reuters · HSBC October 2026 What's your take? Basesh U Gala 1w Report this post INDIA’S BUSINESSES ARE GROWING. BUT ARE THEY CREATING MORE JOBS? India’s private-sector activity hit a four-month high in October. Yet hiring growth slowed to its weakest pace of the year. The HSBC Flash PMI rose from 55.9 to 56.7, signalling stronger business activity. But employment increased only marginally. Business activity is accelerating. But hiring isn’t keeping pace. This raises an important question for every entrepreneur: Is your business growing because your team is becoming more productive or because your existing employees are carrying more work? These are not the same thing. When orders increase, hiring without planning can raise costs. But delaying necessary hiring can exhaust your team, weaken customer service and limit growth. Both decisions have consequences. For MSMEs, the solution isn't simply to hire more people or expect fewer people to do more. It's to build the capacity to grow. → Measure productivity. Identify bottlenecks that waste time, money and effort. → Develop your people. Set clear responsibilities, improve skills and prepare employees for greater responsibility. → Strengthen systems. Use SOPs and technology to reduce repetitive work and dependence on the founder. → Hire strategically. When demand is sustained and your team approaches its capacity, hire before service quality suffers. Remember, technology should help people work smarter not become an excuse to overload them. A business isn't truly stronger simply because revenue grows. It's stronger when its people, processes and capacity grow with it.
